name: Marcus Aurelius
info: Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and a Stoic philosopher, the last of the Five Good Emperors, whose reign saw the Parthian and Marcomannic wars and the Antonine Plague and who wrote the Meditations.

facts.born: 26 April 121, in Rome; son of the praetor Marcus Annius Verus and Domitia Lucilla, of the gens Annia, related by marriage to Trajan and Hadrian
facts.died: 17 March 180, of unknown causes, in his military quarters at Vindobona or near Sirmium, at the age of 58
facts.role: Consul in 140, 145 and 161; Caesar and heir of Antoninus Pius from 138; Roman emperor from 161 to 180, jointly with Lucius Verus until 169 and with Commodus from 177
facts.known: the Meditations; Stoic philosophy; the Marcomannic Wars; the Parthian War of Lucius Verus; the Antonine Plague; the Column of Marcus Aurelius and his equestrian statue

t: Adopted by Antoninus Pius at Hadrian's wish in 138, Marcus was trained for rule for over twenty years and on his accession in 161 insisted on sharing power with his adoptive brother Lucius Verus.
His reign was taken up by war with Parthia in the east and with the Marcomanni, Quadi and Iazyges on the Danube, while the Antonine Plague killed five to ten million people.
The Meditations, written in Greek on campaign for his own guidance, made him the model of the philosopher king, though historians have criticised his choice of Commodus as successor.
dyk: The bronze equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius, made in c. 175 and now in the Capitoline Museums, is the only Roman equestrian statue to have survived into the modern period.
ev: Hadrian chooses Antoninus as heir on condition that he adopt Marcus and Lucius
Marcus marries Faustina, the daughter of Antoninus
Antoninus dies and Marcus becomes emperor with Lucius Verus, the first time Rome is ruled by two emperors
Roman forces take Ctesiphon and sack Seleucia; the Antonine Plague breaks out in 165 or 166
The Marcomanni and other Germanic peoples cross the Danube, opening the Marcomannic Wars
Lucius Verus dies, probably of the plague, on the way back to Rome
Marcus begins to rule jointly with his son Commodus
Marcus dies on campaign and is succeeded by Commodus

sections.early:
Marcus was born in Rome on 26 April 121, the son of the praetor Marcus Annius Verus and Domitia Lucilla. The Annii Veri, of Italic origin, had settled at Ucubi in Baetica and risen to prominence in Rome in the late 1st century; through his grandmother Rupilia Faustina he was related to the Nerva-Antonine dynasty. His mother had inherited a great fortune, including brickworks outside Rome and a villa on the Caelian Hill, where he grew up. His father probably died in 125 or 126, and Marcus was raised by his grandfather, Marcus Annius Verus, with help from Lucius Catilius Severus.

He was educated at home. He trained in wrestling and boxing and joined the Salii, priests of Mars. His teacher Diognetus seems to have introduced him to the philosophic way of life, and in April 132 he took up a philosopher's rough cloak and slept on the ground until his mother persuaded him to use a bed. Later tutors included Alexander of Cotiaeum, the Greek orators Herodes Atticus and the Latin orator Marcus Cornelius Fronto, with whom he kept a close and affectionate correspondence. Against Fronto's warnings, Apollonius of Chalcedon and above all Quintus Junius Rusticus drew him to Stoicism; by 146 or 147 he had grown tired of his studies in rhetoric and jurisprudence.
sections.rise:
Hadrian, who had first chosen Lucius Aelius Caesar as heir, turned after Aelius died in 138 to Antoninus, the husband of Marcus's aunt Faustina the Elder. On 24 January 138 Antoninus was named successor on condition that he adopt both Marcus and Lucius, the son of Aelius; it would appear that Hadrian intended Marcus eventually to rule. Marcus reportedly greeted the news with sadness. When Hadrian died on 10 July 138, Antoninus, soon called Pius, broke off Marcus's betrothal to Ceionia Fabia and betrothed him to his own daughter Faustina, whom he married in April 145.

As heir Marcus was consul in 140 and again in 145, became princeps iuventutis and joined the priestly colleges, and was made to live in the palace on the Palatine, where he struggled to reconcile court life with philosophy. On 1 December 147, the day after his first child was born, Antoninus gave him the tribunician power and the imperium. He took on more administrative work as Antoninus aged. When Antoninus died on 7 March 161, the Senate planned to confirm Marcus alone, but he refused office unless Lucius received equal powers; Lucius took the name Lucius Aurelius Verus. It was the first time Rome was ruled by two emperors, though Marcus held more authority. They promised the Praetorian Guard a donative of 20,000 sesterces each, twice the usual size.
sections.deeds:
The early reign was popular: the emperors were praised for behaviour lacking pomp and permitted free speech, and new provisions were made for poor children. War soon followed. In 161 Vologases IV of Parthia installed his own king in Armenia and destroyed a Roman legion at Elegeia. Lucius went east to direct the war in 162 while Marcus stayed in Rome. Artaxata fell in 163, a new king was installed in Armenia, and in 165 Avidius Cassius took Ctesiphon, burning its palace, and sacked Seleucia, which had opened its gates. From 166 the Marcomanni, Lombards, Iazyges and Costoboci crossed the northern frontier; in 168 the two emperors drove the Marcomanni and Quadi from Aquileia, and after a long struggle Marcus pushed the invaders back.

Like other emperors, he spent much of his time on petitions and disputes. Jurists called him "an emperor most skilled in the law", and he showed marked interest in the manumission of slaves, the guardianship of orphans and minors and the choice of city councillors. He routinely asked the Senate's permission to spend money. On his accession he reduced the silver purity of the denarius from 83.5% to 79%; he raised it to 82% in 168 and returned to the lower value two years later because of the military crises. In 166 a traveller reached the Han court claiming to represent "Andun", ruler of Daqin, who may be Marcus or Antoninus.
sections.opponents:
The reign's troubles came less from rivals at court than from war, disease and the empire's borders. The Antonine Plague, which began in Mesopotamia in 165 or 166 and is believed to have been smallpox, killed five to ten million people; Raoul McLaughlin argues it did irreparable damage to Roman trade in the Indian Ocean. The sack of Seleucia left a black mark on Lucius's reputation, and an official excuse was found that the Seleucids broke faith first. Germanic settlers who had been brought into Italy seized Ravenna, after which Marcus banished those settled there. Marcus himself had no military experience at his accession, and his choice of a reliable rather than a talented man, his cousin Annius Libo, for Syria has been noted.

The persecution of Christians seemingly increased in number and severity during the reign, though how far the emperor directed, encouraged or knew of it is much debated. In the Meditations he criticised what he saw as the Christians' theatrical approach to martyrdom. A letter in Justin Martyr's First Apology in which Marcus credits Christian prayer for a "rain miracle" and asks the Senate to end persecution is widely considered inauthentic; Cassius Dio attributes the miracle to an Egyptian magician, Harnuphis. The main sources are patchy: the Historia Augusta, probably by one author of about 395, and Cassius Dio, whose senatorial prejudices obscure his view.
sections.last:
Lucius Verus fell ill and died on the way back to Rome in January or February 169, probably of the plague, leaving Marcus sole emperor during the northern wars. Between 170 and 180, while on campaign, he wrote the Meditations in Greek as a guide for himself. Large numbers of Germanic settlers in the frontier regions required the creation of two new provinces beyond the Danube, Sarmatia and Marcomannia, and his victory over the Sarmatians and Germanic tribes in 176 was later commemorated by a column in Rome.

Marcus had named his sons Annius and Commodus as heirs in 166, and from 177 he ruled jointly with Commodus. He died at the age of 58 on 17 March 180, of unknown causes, in his military quarters either at Vindobona or near Sirmium. He was immediately deified, and his ashes rested in Hadrian's mausoleum until the Visigoth sack of Rome in 410. Commodus was only the second son by birth, after Titus, to succeed his father. Historians have criticised the succession, citing Commodus's erratic behaviour and lack of political and military skill; Michael Grant argued that rejecting his son's claim would almost certainly have meant civil war. Some scholars consider Marcus's death the end of the Pax Romana.
sections.legacy:
Marcus had the reputation of a philosopher king in his own lifetime. Cassius Dio and the Historia Augusta both call him "the philosopher", and Christian writers such as Justin Martyr, Athenagoras and Eusebius gave him the title too. Dio ended his account of the reign with praise, writing that amid extraordinary difficulties he survived and preserved the empire, and that history then "descends from a kingdom of gold to one of iron and rust". Herodian wrote that alone of the emperors he proved his learning by his blameless character. Iain King has called his legacy tragic, since the imperial line he anointed abandoned his Stoic philosophy.

The Meditations survived in the scholarly tradition of the Eastern Church, are first quoted by Arethas of Caesarea in the 10th century and were first printed by Wilhelm Xylander at Zurich in 1558; the oldest complete manuscript, in the Vatican, dates from the 14th century. The book is one of the most important sources for ancient Stoicism, was a favourite of Frederick the Great, John Stuart Mill, Matthew Arnold and Goethe, and sold 100,000 copies in 2019. In Rome his column, completed in 193, carries a spiral of reliefs of his campaigns, and his bronze equestrian statue of c. 175, with a hand outstretched in clemency, is the only Roman equestrian statue to survive.

summary: Marcus Aurelius, adopted heir of Antoninus Pius, ruled Rome from 161 to 180, first with Lucius Verus. His reign was spent largely at war with Parthia and on the Danube while the Antonine Plague swept the empire. His Meditations made him the model of the Stoic philosopher king, though his succession by Commodus has been criticised.
